title: Lyra Capital - Dedicated Capacity Discovery
header:
Date: 2026-04-07
Start time: 14:30 PDT
Duration: 47 minutes
Recording: https://app.fireflies.ai/recordings/ff-20260407-lyra-001
Attendees: Alex Morgan (Redwood AE), Diego Ruiz (Redwood SE), Maya Chen (Lyra, Head of ML), Tom Reynolds (Lyra, CTO), Sofia Patel (Lyra, Infra Lead)
summary: Discovery call to evaluate Redwood Dedicated for Lyra Capital's high-throughput inference workloads. Focus: reserved GPU sizing, isolation/data controls, burst strategy and autoscaling, expected latency/cost tradeoffs, and compliance requirements (SOC 2, SSO/SAML, KMS). Agreed next steps: send detailed Dedicated pricing + capacity options, security docs, and schedule a 2-week benchmark pilot in a dedicated pool.
action_items: Alex Morgan - Send Dedicated pricing, capacity tiers, and burst policy examples - due 2026-04-09
Diego Ruiz - Share benchmark template and sample KV cache configs - due 2026-04-10
Maya Chen - Provide representative request traces and 7-day traffic peaks - due 2026-04-12
Sofia Patel - Share network/VPC requirements and KMS details - due 2026-04-12
next_steps: Redwood to email pricing and security pack (SOC2/ISO docs, SSO guide)
Lyra to provide sample traffic and keys for benchmark environment
Align procurement timeline (aiming for Dedicated contract signed by end of Q2 2026)
transcript:
00:00 Alex Morgan: hey everyone thanks for joining, uh we can wait another minute for others but I think we have the core team.
00:12 Maya Chen: yeah works for us, thanks Alex.
00:15 Alex Morgan: great, quick intro — I'm Alex Morgan here on Redwood's account team, and Diego Ruiz is our solutions engineer. Diego quick wave?
00:22 Diego Ruiz: hey hi, uh Diego here, I'll be covering the technical side — latency, autoscaling, kernels, that sort of thing.
00:27 Tom Reynolds: Tom here, CTO. We run inference for a few portfolio products, mainly low-latency scoring and batch embed pipelines.
00:35 Sofia Patel: Sofia infra lead, i'll handle network and security questions.
00:38 Alex Morgan: Awesome. Goal for today is to understand your workload and figure out whether Dedicated or Private makes most sense, sizing reserved GPUs, and how you want burst capacity and scaling.
01:02 Maya Chen: Cool. For context we currently run a mix — some models on hosted LLM APIs and some on prem GPUs. We're looking to consolidate to a single inference provider for predictable costs and support. Our primary concerns are isolation (data control), consistent latency around 80-120ms p50 for text generation, and handling bursts up to 2-3x baseline qps.
01:28 Diego Ruiz: Got it. Can you share baseline numbers — tokens per second, average sequence length, and peak qps?
01:35 Maya Chen: Baseline is roughly 200 qps across a few endpoints, peaks up to 600 qps during market open windows. Sequence length average 120 tokens, but we have some 400 token tails for long docs.
01:48 Tom Reynolds: Important: we can't have data co-mingled with other customers. SOC 2 and audit logs are required. We also want SAML SSO integration and KMS for key management.
02:02 Diego Ruiz: That's standard for Dedicated. Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools with tenant isolation, VPC peering or private connectivity. We also support private on-prem installs if you need full air-gapped.
02:15 Sofia Patel: For connectivity, we prefer VPC peering + customer-managed KMS. Does Redwood support bringing our own KMS/HSM?
02:22 Alex Morgan: Yes, we integrate with common KMS providers and support bring-your-own via HSM integrations for Private. For Dedicated we can also integrate KMS.
02:30 Maya Chen: Ok. Can you talk about burst strategy — we need predictable capacity during spikes without paying for 3x reserved GPUs.
02:38 Diego Ruiz: Sure. We recommend a capacity model: reserved baseline (committed GPUs) sized for your p95 steady state, plus burst pool — typically a shared elastic pool you can draw from. You can define burst policies by route. During a spike we can route non-critical requests to cheaper models or older quantized variants. There's also automatic fallback if the primary model is saturated.
02:58 Tom Reynolds: How fast does burst capacity scale? We're sensitive to cold start times.
03:04 Diego Ruiz: Burst GPUs are warm, not cold — they keep model weights resident for common variants. Scaling is usually in tens of seconds, not minutes; we've optimized kernel selection and KV cache warm-up to reduce ramp. For your 2-3x spikes we'd recommend a baseline sized at ~60-70% of your typical peak and provisioning burst to cover the rest.
03:25 Maya Chen: That sounds promising. Any constraints on model size or quantization we should be aware of? We run a 16B LLM for scoring and a few 70B models for advanced use cases.
03:35 Diego Ruiz: Dedicated supports 16B and 70B families. For 70B we typically suggest 8-bit quant or Triton-style kernels depending on hardware. For consistent latency we can pin the model to specific instance types. We also have recommendations for KV cache management to keep latency low for long sequence lengths.
03:54 Sofia Patel: About runbooks and observability — we need token-level cost, per-route latency and tracing, and audit logs forwarded to our SIEM.
04:03 Alex Morgan: Redwood Console exposes per-route metrics, token breakdowns, tracing hooks, and can forward logs to your SIEM via secure endpoints. Audit logs and retention policies can be configured to meet compliance.
04:15 Tom Reynolds: Procurement question — what's the usual contract structure for Dedicated? Monthly reserved capacity with burst metered?
04:23 Alex Morgan: Typically it's reserved capacity (monthly or annual commit) for baseline GPUs. Bursts are either included as a fixed buffer or metered as overage, depending on the contract. We can model cost for your traffic profile and show TCO versus on-prem or fully hosted.
04:36 Maya Chen: Can you send a cost model? We need CAPEX vs OPEX numbers.
04:41 Alex Morgan: Yes, action item — we'll send pricing scenarios and a modeled TCO for your 200 qps baseline and 600 qps peak.
04:48 Maya Chen: Great. On security: we need SOC 2 Type II, ISO certs, SSO via SAML, RBAC, and support for customer-managed KMS. Also data residency — logs must stay in our AWS account.
05:01 Diego Ruiz: We support SOC 2 and ISO docs. For data residency we can either deploy a dedicated control plane in your region or provide Private deployment. Logs can be forwarded to your account via direct log sinks.
05:14 Tom Reynolds: If we choose Dedicated, what does the onboarding look like and how long to production?
05:20 Alex Morgan: Onboarding is typically 4-8 weeks depending on complexity — baseline provisioning, networking (VPC peering), security reviews, and a pilot/benchmark. For simple cases it's 4 weeks; for stricter security controls or private installs it's longer.
05:32 Maya Chen: We want to run a 2-week pilot benchmark with our traces, can you support that?
05:37 Diego Ruiz: Yes. We'll set up a dedicated pool for the pilot, run your traffic, and collect latency and cost metrics. We'll also test burst behavior and fallback policies.
05:48 Sofia Patel: For the pilot, what credentials do you need and how is data handled? We can't share PII or keys in the clear.
05:55 Diego Ruiz: We'll provide a secure upload mechanism for traces and a short-lived keypair for the pilot environment. Data handling is covered under our NDA and we can redact PII as part of the benchmark.
06:06 Tom Reynolds: Any reference customers in finance who use Dedicated?
06:10 Alex Morgan: Yes, a few tier-2 banks and trading platforms — we can share anonymized case studies.
06:15 Maya Chen: One thing: some words recognized as K-V cash in past transcripts — we want to ensure the KV cache warm-up is fast because of our long sequences.
06:24 Diego Ruiz: Right — KV cache warm-up is handled with prefetch heuristics and we persist hot KV shards to reduce warm latency. For your workload with long tails we can prepopulate KV for common prefixes.
06:36 Tom Reynolds: How about monitoring and escalation — we need SLOs and an on-call path.
06:41 Alex Morgan: Dedicated comes with an SLA for uptime and latency targets; we also offer 24/7 support for enterprise tiers with a direct on-call pager.
06:50 Maya Chen: Are there known tradeoffs between Dedicated and Private for our use case?
06:53 Diego Ruiz: Dedicated gives the best balance: you get isolation, predictable performance, and Redwood manages infra. Private (on-prem) is for full control and air-gapped needs but adds ops overhead and longer lead times. Hosted is fastest but less isolated.
07:08 Sofia Patel: For network topology — will we do VPC peering or private link?
07:12 Diego Ruiz: Both supported. Peering is simpler; PrivateLink adds an extra security boundary. We'll map options in the security pack.
07:20 Maya Chen: Ok let's talk numbers — Diego what size gpui pool would you recommend for our 200 qps baseline and 600 peak with 70B occasional loads?
07:29 Diego Ruiz: Rough back-of-envelope: for 16B family, one A100 80GB equiv can handle ~50-80 qps depending on batching. For your baseline 200 qps, I'd recommend 3-4 GPUs reserved for 16B workloads. For 70B we suggest separate pool with quantized variants — each node might do 10-20 qps; you'd need a handful, or route less latency-sensitive traffic to quantized variants. Combined, baseline reserve of ~8 GPUs with burst capacity up to 16 GPUs would be a reasonable starting point. We'll run numbers in the cost model.
08:03 Tom Reynolds: That's helpful. Any constraints on software stack — do you support Kubernetes sidecars or do we call Redwood API?
08:10 Diego Ruiz: You call Redwood API. For Private we can provide connectors or run in your cluster. For Dedicated we provide a secure endpoint and SDKs.
08:19 Maya Chen: About model versioning and rollouts — can we pin a model and do canary?
08:23 Alex Morgan: Yes, Redwood supports model pinning, canary rollouts, A/B tests and automatic fallback policies.
08:30 Sofia Patel: For audit we need per-token logs for 90 days — is that configurable?
08:35 Alex Morgan: Yes, retention and log forwarding is configurable; longer retention available as an add-on.
08:40 Tom Reynolds: Ok, next steps recap?
08:43 Alex Morgan: We'll send: 1) Dedicated pricing and capacity scenarios, 2) security pack (SOC2, SAML guide, KMS integration), 3) benchmark template and pilot plan. Diego will own the benchmark template. Maya and Sofia will share traffic traces and network requirements.
08:58 Maya Chen: Sounds good. Aim to kick off pilot week of Apr 20. Procurement aiming for end of Q2.
09:05 Alex Morgan: Great — thanks everyone. We'll follow up by email with the doc set and calendar invites.
09:12 Tom Reynolds: Thanks all.
09:14 Sofia Patel: Bye.
09:15 [meeting ends]
